1:
Nobody can date the psalm. Calvin says so plainly: it is anonymous, "nor can we, with certainty, determine to what time it relates." He reports two conjectures — Hezekiah's deliverance from the Assyrian army, or the opening of the temple after the return from Babylon — admits "we have nothing but conjecture to offer", and prefers the second. Clarke goes through the versions and finds no author at all: the psalm "is not attributed to David" by the Hebrew or by any ancient version save one — "the Arabic alone prefixes the name of David." Several call it a psalm of the resurrection, "but for this there is no authority". Clarke himself reads the Babylonian return throughout, addressing "all ye people who, from different parts of the Babylonish empire, are now on return to your own land."

Delitzsch works from position rather than occasion. The psalm belongs to a series linked "according to the community of prominent watchwords" — the vow paid in the psalm before, the vows paid here. He notices something about the heading too: of the fifty-five psalms carrying "to the chief musician", these two alone are anonymous. Gill escapes the dating problem by referring the psalm forward, to the Messiah and the latter day.

What the joyful noise is gets four answers. Ellicott gives the plain one: "better, sing aloud, or shout." Augustine gives the technical one, the most exact description in the chapter: "jubilation is not of words, but the sound alone of men rejoicing is uttered, as of a heart labouring and bringing forth into voice the pleasure of a thing imagined which cannot be expressed." Spurgeon makes it a matter of setting: in Zion, where the instructed saints meditated, "the song was silent unto God", but in the great popular assemblies a joyful noise was fitter — though "we need not so much noise, as joyful noise." Henry unfolds it into four: God's glory, man's duty, a prediction of the conversion of the Gentiles, and the poet's good-will.

Augustine turns the words "all lands" against the divided. Since the psalm addresses every land and "not therefore Judaea alone", he mourns most those "that being gathered together have been divided": "let no one jubilate in a part... whosoever holdeth a part and from the whole is cut off, should howl, not jubilate." Henry hears the same publicity from the other end: praise must be "open and public, as those that are not ashamed of our Master".

Ellicott suspects the text itself in the second verse. "Sing forth" is "literally, play on the harp"; the third verse then opens so baldly that "a suspicion arises as to the arrangement of the text", repaired by moving its first words back: "ascribe glory (and) speak praise to God." Clarke reads the submission that follows more sharply: the enemies "literally, lie unto thee", as Pharaoh did, who "promised again and again to let the people go" and "as frequently falsified their word." On the worship of all the earth he narrows the scope to the land and claims the fulfilment as historical: "there shall no more an idol be found among the tribes of Israel... After the Babylonish captivity the Israelites never relapsed into idolatry."

The verb of the crossing divides them by mood. Delitzsch judges the future rendering "unnatural", the cohortative being referable to the past where the writer "throws himself back". Ellicott holds the opposite: "the verb is properly optative — there... let us rejoice", which "is more in keeping with the first verses of the psalm". He also corrects the flood, a word that "generally stands for the Euphrates" but here means the Jordan or the Red Sea, and makes the watching eyes military: "God is, as it were, Israel's outpost, ever on the alert." Wesley claims the memory for the living: "our nation, or our ancestors, in whose loins we then were."
8:
The call narrows from all lands to one people, and both preachers notice it. Henry puts it as a question: praise should be heard from Israel above all, "for from whom should it be heard but from those who are his peculiar favourites and select attendants?" Spurgeon presses it into precedence — "first visited by his love, ye should be foremost in his praise" — then out again: "compel unwilling ears to hear the praises of your covenant God."

What it is to be held in life is where they part company. Ellicott gives the plain construction, "which putteth our soul into life, i.e., keeps us alive, as the parallelism shows"; Clarke reads it the same way, adding what is preserved: "we have our life, our liberty, and our religion." Henry stays with natural preservation too, and makes it precarious: God holds the soul in life "that it may not drop away of itself; for, being continually in our hands, it is apt to slip through our fingers", since "his providence is a continued creation". He raises the standard too: "it is not existence, but happiness, that deserves the name of life." Gill refuses the whole reading: the clause "is not to be understood of infusing a living soul in man, nor of the preservation of natural life, which is common to all men", but of eternal life ordained and procured. Spurgeon takes the second clause as the greater gift: "immortal and immovable are those whom God preserves. Satan is put to shame, for instead of being able to slay the saints, he is not even able to trip them up."

The trying of silver is read as metallurgy. Clarke explains the figure as "taken from melting and refining metals", used "especially to represent cases where there is doubt concerning the purity of the metal, the quantity of alloy, or even the nature or kind." Delitzsch keeps the furnace but shifts the purpose: God "has cast His people as it were into a smelting-furnace or fining-pot in order to purify and to prove them by suffering", a figure he notes as a favourite of Isaiah's. Gill takes the result rather than the process: the proving found their grace "not reprobate silver... but of the right kind".

The net is contested. Ellicott concedes that the Hebrew word "certainly means net" elsewhere, and that the ancient versions render it so here, but reports that other ancient translators "prefer the usual meaning, stronghold", which "is more in keeping with the other images of violence and oppression": "the fortress, the hard labour, the subjection as by foes riding over the vanquished, the passage through fire and water, all raise a picture of the direst tyranny." Clarke keeps the net and finds it in the exodus, where Pharaoh said "the wilderness hath shut them in, — they are entangled", "comparing their state to that of a wild beast in a net"; the affliction on the loins he takes physiologically, for "that sharp pain in the back and loins which is generally felt on the apprehension of sudden danger."

Clarke supplies the military picture for the riding: the people are treated "as broken infantry are when the cavalry dashes among their disordered ranks". Gill notices that the Hebrew is singular — "a man", a frail mortal man — and applies it to the man of sin.

Where they are brought out to is a third disagreement. Clarke reads the wealthy place geographically, as a "well watered place, to wit, the land of Judea", and quotes an old psalter for the passage through fire and water: the trials are gone through "as a man that leves noght his waye for hete na for kald, for dry na for wette". Ellicott prefers the ancient versions' "to refreshment", "certainly more in keeping with the figures employed", while allowing that "a slight change gives the frequent figure, a broad place."
13:
The psalm changes from plural to singular here, and they divide over whether the singular is real. Ellicott says it cannot be: "such a holocaust could hardly have been vowed by a single person. It is the community that speaks." The ram, besides, "was not a sacrifice for any individual, but particularly enjoined for the high priest", a tribal head, or a Nazarite. Wesley says the same in a line: "one speaks in the name of all the rest." Delitzsch splits the difference: the poet speaks for himself "but, as the diversity and the kind of the sacrifices show, as being a member of the community at large." Spurgeon holds the opposite, and makes the singular the point: "the child of God is so sensible of his own personal indebtedness to grace, that he feels he must utter a song of his own... since the best public form must fail to meet each individual case."

Henry reads the offerings as expense. Not everyone could afford them, and some "wanted zeal to be at such an expense in praising God"; the psalmist chooses burnt-sacrifices, of which "the offerer had no share". The rule is short: "God, who is the best, must be served with the best we have." Gill agrees on the grade, "of the fattest of the flock; that is, of the best"; Clarke states the exclusion: "the lame and the blind shall never be given to thee for sacrifice."

Clarke fixes the passage to the return: "now that thou hast restored us to our own land, and established us in it, we will establish thy worship", the vows being those of exile — "we often vowed, if thou wouldst deliver us from our bondage, to worship and serve thee alone." He then quotes an old psalter for a turn he approves, the vows being confessions "that I am noght, and thou arte all: and I hafe nede of the, noght thou of me" — "a right distinction."

What was uttered is put two ways. Ellicott and Gill take the verb at its root, "literally, opened", and Gill draws the consequence: the vow was "publicly and distinctly declared, and from which there is no going back". Spurgeon hears something less deliberate: the words were "blurted out, as we say in common speech."

The trouble that produced the vows is treated as suspect. Clarke is blunt about the pattern: distress "is generally the time when good resolutions are formed, and vows made; but how often are these forgotten when affliction and calamity are removed!" Henry puts it positively: "we do not acceptably praise God for our deliverance out of trouble unless we make conscience of paying the vows we made when we were in trouble." Spurgeon supplies both caution and argument: "we should be slow in making vows, but prompt in discharging them", and "how can we hope for help another time, if we prove faithless to covenants voluntarily entered upon in hours of need?" He refuses the offerer any credit: "our largest gifts are but payments."

On the incense of rams they converge without quite agreeing on the grammar. Henry takes it as the fat of rams, "which being burnt upon the altar, the smoke of it would ascend like the smoke of incense", while allowing the alternative "rams with incense". Clarke describes it physically, "the fine effluvia arising from the burning of the pure fat"; Ellicott states flatly that "incense is here the ascending smoke of the sacrifice"; Wesley makes the equivalence the point, the fat being "no less pleasing to God than incense". Henry alone looks past the smoke to what it stands for: "the incense typifies Christ's intercession, without which the fattest of our sacrifices will not be accepted." Spurgeon says the same of the victim: "never attempt to come before God without Jesus, the divinely promised, given, and accepted burnt offering."
16:
The summons changes verb, and Spurgeon builds on the change: "before, they were bidden to come and see. Hearing is faith's seeing... They saw how terrible God was, but they heard how gracious he was." Where they differ is over how wide the call reaches. Spurgeon reads the qualification as a restriction, and enforces it: the God-fearing "are a fit audience when a good man is about to relate his experience; and it is well to select our hearers when inward soul matters are our theme." Gill agrees, in the same figure of pearls before swine. Delitzsch reads it as a description of extent rather than a filter: the words "are addressed in the widest extent... to all who fear God, wheresoever such are to be found on the face of the earth."

Why it should be told at all is answered practically. Clarke says the psalmist means "to teach them by example, more powerful always than precept". Spurgeon makes it an obligation on the mature, so "that the younger and feebler sort may be encouraged", and insists on first-hand testimony: "second-hand experience is like cauld kale het again." What is not worth telling is human achievement — "there are trumpeters enough of man's trumpery deeds."

The praying is described as audible: Gill notes that "crying with the mouth denotes vocal, ardent, and fervent prayer", Delitzsch that it was "not merely silently in spirit, but audibly and importunately". Ellicott catches an idiom in the second clause: literally "exaltation was under my tongue, apparently a Hebrew idiom akin to our on the tip of the tongue, i.e., ready at any moment for utterance." Clarke matches the halves: God "as graciously received my thanksgiving, as he compassionately heard my prayer."

The condition about iniquity is the real difficulty, and Gill takes the most care over it. There is iniquity in the psalmist's heart, "as there is in every good man's heart, and a great deal too"; indeed it "should be regarded in some sense, so as to guard against it... and so as to loath it, abhor it" — but not "so as to nourish and cherish it." The verb, he adds, may be rendered "if I look upon it", that is, "with approbation of it".

Ellicott sharpens the same point into a tense and an epigram: "if I had seen evil (i.e., had had it purposely in view) in my heart, the Lord would not have heard me. One may not be pardoned and retain the offence." He allows two references — "the forming of wicked schemes, or... the complacent view of wickedness in others" — and draws a dating conclusion nobody else draws: "the protestation of innocence in this verse, being made by or for the community at large, marks a late period for the composition." Clarke locates the fault in pretence — "if I pretended to be what I was not; if I loved iniquity, while I professed to pray and be sorry for my sin" — Wesley in the interior alone: "if my heart had been false to God, although I might have forborne outward acts."

The last verses run the argument backwards. Gill takes the answered prayer as proof of the character: God heard, "so that it was a plain case that he had not regarded iniquity in his heart; had not lived a vicious course of life, nor was an hypocrite." On the closing blessing he specifies what did not happen: God has "not been angry against it, shut it out, or covered himself with a cloud that it might not pass through". Ellicott reads the same negative as a fact about the psalmist — "he found himself able to pray, was not silenced" — and notes the zeugma by which one verb carries both prayer and mercy. Clarke closes the circle: "thus he told them what God had done for his soul."
